passage.title: The Myth of the Multitasker
passage.text: Few claims are made as confidently in job interviews as the ability to multitask. Yet decades of research in cognitive psychology suggest that what most of us call multitasking is, in fact, something rather different: rapid switching between tasks, each switch carrying a small but measurable cost. When we move our attention from an email to a spreadsheet and back again, the brain must disengage from one set of rules and reload another. Individually, these delays last only fractions of a second. Accumulated over a working day, however, they can amount to a substantial loss of productive time. More troubling still is the finding that people who consider themselves skilled multitaskers often perform worse on tests of attention than those who do not. In one well-known series of experiments, heavy media users were more easily distracted by irrelevant information and slower to switch between tasks, precisely the abilities they believed they excelled at. The researchers were careful not to claim that media use causes poor concentration; it may simply be that easily distracted people are drawn to juggling several screens at once. Either way, confidence proved to be a poor guide to competence. None of this means that doing two things simultaneously is always impossible. Walking while talking, or listening to music while cooking, poses little difficulty, because at least one of the activities has become largely automatic. Problems arise when both tasks demand conscious thought. It is for this reason that safety experts have consistently argued that hands-free phones offer little real protection to drivers: the danger lies not in the hands but in the divided mind. For employers, the implications are clear, if not always welcome. Open-plan offices and constant messaging may create an impression of busy efficiency, while quietly eroding the deep concentration on which complex work depends.

passage.title: Rewilding: Letting Nature Take the Lead
passage.text: For much of the twentieth century, conservation in Europe meant management: hedges were trimmed, meadows mown and invasive species removed in an effort to preserve landscapes in a particular, often idealised, state. In recent years, however, a more radical philosophy has gained ground. Rewilding, as it is known, asks what would happen if humans simply stepped back and allowed natural processes to reshape the land. Its advocates point to striking successes. On one former farming estate in southern England, the owners stopped cultivating the land, introduced small herds of free-roaming cattle, pigs and ponies, and then largely left them to it. Within two decades, the estate had become home to rare birds and butterflies that had vanished from the surrounding countryside. Crucially, these species were not deliberately reintroduced; they arrived of their own accord once suitable habitats had emerged. Critics, though, are far from convinced. Some farmers fear that rewilding amounts to abandoning productive land at a time when food security is a growing concern. Others object to the reintroduction of predators such as wolves and lynx, arguing that the risks to livestock are dismissed too lightly by enthusiasts who do not themselves depend on the land for a living. There is also a philosophical objection: if every European landscape has been shaped by human activity for thousands of years, which version of 'wild' are we trying to restore? Perhaps the most persuasive defence of rewilding is a modest one. It need not replace farming or traditional conservation, its more thoughtful supporters argue, but rather complement them. Even small areas left to develop naturally can act as stepping stones, allowing wildlife to move between isolated habitats. Seen in this light, rewilding is less a rejection of human involvement than a recognition that, occasionally, the most effective intervention is restraint.

passage.title: The Hidden Cost of Free
passage.text: There is a curious asymmetry in the way we respond to prices. Reducing the cost of a chocolate from ten cents to five barely changes our behaviour, yet reducing it from one cent to zero can transform it. Behavioural economists have repeatedly found that the word 'free' exerts a pull out of all proportion to the money actually saved. In one classic study, shoppers were offered a choice between a cheap ordinary chocolate and a far superior one at a modest price. Most chose the better chocolate. When both prices were lowered by exactly the same amount, making the ordinary one free, preferences reversed dramatically, even though the difference in price between the two remained identical. Rational calculation, it seems, gives way to something closer to emotion. This insight has not been lost on businesses. Much of the digital economy is built on services that cost the user nothing at the point of use. Search engines, social networks and countless apps are offered free of charge, and their popularity is partly explained by our reluctance to pay even trivial amounts. Yet, as the saying goes, if you are not paying for the product, you are the product. The real price is paid in attention and personal data, both of which are harvested and sold to advertisers. Because this cost is invisible at the moment of choice, users rarely weigh it as they would a cash payment. Some economists argue that this matters less than critics suggest, since most people appear content with the bargain. Others contend that genuine consent is impossible when the terms of the exchange are buried in documents few people read. What is beyond dispute is that 'free' is seldom quite what it appears. Recognising its psychological power may be the first step towards making more deliberate choices about what we are really willing to give up.

passage.title: Why Languages Disappear
passage.text: Of the roughly seven thousand languages spoken today, linguists estimate that as many as half may fall silent by the end of this century. Unlike the extinction of a plant or animal, the death of a language rarely makes headlines, partly because it tends to happen quietly, within a single household, as parents decide which language to pass on to their children. The reasons behind such decisions are seldom irrational. Where one language offers access to education, employment and social mobility, families understandably favour it, and the minority language gradually retreats to the kitchen and the village festival. Within two or three generations, it may be spoken fluently only by a handful of elderly people. Why should this concern the rest of us? One argument is scientific. Each language encodes a distinctive way of organising experience: some have no words for left and right, describing positions instead by compass direction; others classify objects according to their shape. Studying this diversity helps researchers understand the limits and possibilities of human thought. When a language vanishes undocumented, that evidence is lost permanently. Another argument concerns knowledge. Indigenous languages often contain detailed vocabularies for local plants, animals and weather patterns, built up over centuries of close observation. Some of this knowledge has already proved valuable to medicine and ecology. Yet perhaps the most compelling argument is the simplest: for the communities themselves, a language is bound up with identity, memory and dignity. Encouragingly, decline is not inevitable. Hebrew was revived as an everyday spoken language after centuries of being used mainly in religious contexts, and Welsh has made a remarkable recovery thanks to bilingual schooling and broadcasting. Such cases suggest that what ultimately determines a language's survival is not its number of speakers but whether those speakers believe it has a future.

options: It only affects languages without writing systems.

Linguists disagree about how often it happens.
items.explanation: '…it tends to happen quietly, within a single household…'

passage.title: Why Languages Disappear
passage.text: Of the roughly seven thousand languages spoken today, linguists estimate that as many as half may fall silent by the end of this century. Unlike the extinction of a plant or animal, the death of a language rarely makes headlines, partly because it tends to happen quietly, within a single household, as parents decide which language to pass on to their children. The reasons behind such decisions are seldom irrational. Where one language offers access to education, employment and social mobility, families understandably favour it, and the minority language gradually retreats to the kitchen and the village festival. Within two or three generations, it may be spoken fluently only by a handful of elderly people. Why should this concern the rest of us? One argument is scientific. Each language encodes a distinctive way of organising experience: some have no words for left and right, describing positions instead by compass direction; others classify objects according to their shape. Studying this diversity helps researchers understand the limits and possibilities of human thought. When a language vanishes undocumented, that evidence is lost permanently. Another argument concerns knowledge. Indigenous languages often contain detailed vocabularies for local plants, animals and weather patterns, built up over centuries of close observation. Some of this knowledge has already proved valuable to medicine and ecology. Yet perhaps the most compelling argument is the simplest: for the communities themselves, a language is bound up with identity, memory and dignity. Encouragingly, decline is not inevitable. Hebrew was revived as an everyday spoken language after centuries of being used mainly in religious contexts, and Welsh has made a remarkable recovery thanks to bilingual schooling and broadcasting. Such cases suggest that what ultimately determines a language's survival is not its number of speakers but whether those speakers believe it has a future.

passage.title: The Algorithm Will See You Now
passage.text: Artificial intelligence is increasingly being used to read medical scans, and early results are impressive. In several trials, software trained on hundreds of thousands of images has detected certain cancers as accurately as experienced specialists, and occasionally more so. Given the shortage of radiologists in many countries, it is easy to see why health services are enthusiastic. A system that never tires, never has a bad day and can review thousands of images overnight appears to offer an obvious solution to growing waiting lists. Yet those closest to the technology urge caution. One concern is that algorithms are only as good as the data on which they are trained. If that data comes mainly from one population, the software may perform less reliably for patients from other backgrounds, and there have already been cases in which tools that excelled in testing struggled once deployed in different hospitals. Another concern is subtler. When a human doctor makes a diagnosis, they can usually explain their reasoning; many AI systems cannot. Should a patient be told they have a serious illness on the basis of a judgement nobody can fully account for? There is also the question of responsibility. If an algorithm misses a tumour, it is far from clear who should be held accountable: the hospital, the software developer or the doctor who accepted its verdict. Perhaps the most realistic vision is not one in which machines replace doctors, but one in which they work alongside them. Some studies suggest that a specialist assisted by AI outperforms either working alone, catching errors that each might have made independently. Achieving this partnership, however, will require more than clever software. It will depend on careful regulation, diverse training data and doctors who understand the tools well enough to know when not to trust them.

passage.title: The Fifteen-Minute City
passage.text: The idea sounds almost too simple to be controversial: cities should be designed so that residents can reach most of what they need, from schools and doctors to shops and parks, within a fifteen-minute walk or bicycle ride. Championed by urban planners in Paris and adopted, in various forms, by cities from Melbourne to Bogotá, the 'fifteen-minute city' promises cleaner air, stronger communities and less time wasted in traffic. Few would object to such goals in principle. In practice, however, the concept has provoked surprisingly fierce opposition. Part of the hostility stems from misunderstanding. In some places, rumours spread online that residents would be forbidden from leaving their neighbourhoods or fined for driving beyond them, claims that bear no relation to what planners have actually proposed. Yet it would be too convenient to dismiss all criticism as conspiracy theory. More measured critics raise legitimate questions about who benefits. If a neighbourhood becomes more pleasant, property prices tend to rise, and the lower-income residents the policy was meant to help may find themselves priced out. There is also a risk that wealthier districts, which already enjoy good local services, will be transformed first, widening rather than narrowing existing inequalities. Moreover, the model sits uneasily with the realities of many people's lives. A nurse working night shifts across the city, or a parent whose child attends a specialist school, cannot simply choose to live and work within the same few streets. For them, restrictions on traffic may feel less like liberation than inconvenience. None of this invalidates the underlying vision. What it suggests is that the fifteen-minute city works best not as a rigid blueprint but as a guiding principle, applied with sensitivity to local circumstances and, above all, developed in genuine consultation with the people who will have to live in it.

passage.title: Rethinking Sleep
passage.text: For generations, the standard advice has been that adults need eight hours of uninterrupted sleep each night. Yet historical research suggests that this ideal may be a relatively recent invention. Drawing on diaries, court records and medical texts, one historian found frequent references in pre-industrial Europe to a 'first sleep' and a 'second sleep', separated by an hour or so of wakefulness in the middle of the night. During this interval, people would pray, tend the fire, talk quietly or simply lie awake reflecting. Far from being regarded as a disorder, the waking period seems to have been an accepted and even valued part of the night. Only with the spread of artificial lighting, which pushed bedtimes later, and the demands of industrial work schedules did the pattern gradually disappear, so that by the twentieth century the very memory of it had faded. This has intriguing implications. Many people today who wake at three in the morning and struggle to fall asleep again assume that something is wrong with them, and the anxiety this generates may make the problem worse. If segmented sleep is, at least for some people, a natural pattern rather than a symptom, the advice they receive might need to change. Sleep scientists, however, are cautious about drawing firm conclusions. Historical sources reveal what people did, not necessarily what was best for them, and modern laboratory studies have produced mixed results. What is clearer is that the total amount of sleep, and its regularity, matter more for health than whether it occurs in one block. Chronic sleep deprivation has been linked to everything from heart disease to impaired memory. Perhaps the most useful lesson, then, is not that we should all adopt medieval sleeping habits, but that a brief period of wakefulness at night is not, in itself, a cause for alarm.

Drawing on diaries, court records and medical texts, one historian found frequent references in pre-industrial Europe to a 'first sleep' and a 'second sleep', separated by an hour or so of wakefulness in the middle of the night. During this interval, people would pray, tend the fire, talk quietly or simply lie awake reflecting. Far from being regarded as a disorder, the waking period seems to have been an accepted and even valued part of the night. Only with the spread of artificial lighting, which pushed bedtimes later, and the demands of industrial work schedules did the pattern gradually disappear, so that by the twentieth century the very memory of it had faded. This has intriguing implications. Many people today who wake at three in the morning and struggle to fall asleep again assume that something is wrong with them, and the anxiety this generates may make the problem worse. If segmented sleep is, at least for some people, a natural pattern rather than a symptom, the advice they receive might need to change. Sleep scientists, however, are cautious about drawing firm conclusions. Historical sources reveal what people did, not necessarily what was best for them, and modern laboratory studies have produced mixed results. What is clearer is that the total amount of sleep, and its regularity, matter more for health than whether it occurs in one block. Chronic sleep deprivation has been linked to everything from heart disease to impaired memory. Perhaps the most useful lesson, then, is not that we should all adopt medieval sleeping habits, but that a brief period of wakefulness at night is not, in itself, a cause for alarm.

passage.title: The Trouble with Grades
passage.text: Ask most teachers why they give grades and they will offer two answers: grades tell students how well they are doing, and they motivate them to do better. Both claims seem self-evident, yet a growing body of research has cast doubt on the second. In a frequently cited study, students who received written comments on their work, without any grade, showed greater improvement in subsequent tasks than those who received a grade alone. More surprisingly, students who received both a grade and comments improved no more than those who received only the grade. The explanation appears to be that once a number or letter is attached, students focus almost exclusively on it, comparing themselves with classmates and ignoring the advice that might actually help them improve. The grade, in other words, ends the conversation about learning rather than continuing it. This finding has prompted some schools to experiment with 'gradeless' classrooms, in which students receive detailed feedback throughout the year and grades are awarded only at the end, if at all. Supporters report that students become more willing to take risks and less anxious about making mistakes. Sceptics, though, raise practical objections. Universities and employers rely on grades to compare applicants quickly, and parents, understandably, want a clear indication of their children's progress. Detailed written feedback is also far more time-consuming for teachers, who are already among the most overworked professionals. A compromise may lie in separating the two functions grades are asked to serve. Feedback during the learning process could focus purely on how to improve, while formal grades are reserved for moments when a summary judgement is genuinely needed. Such an approach would not abolish grades, but it would restore them to their proper role: a record of learning, rather than a substitute for it.

passage.title: Whose Treasures?
passage.text: Walk through the great museums of Europe and North America and you will encounter objects from every corner of the globe: bronze sculptures from West Africa, marble carvings from ancient Greece, ceremonial masks from the Pacific. For many visitors, these collections represent the best of human achievement gathered under one roof. For a growing number of critics, however, they also represent something less comfortable. A significant proportion of these objects were acquired during the colonial era, sometimes through purchase or exchange but often through military conquest or under conditions in which the original owners had little genuine choice. Calls for their return, known as restitution, have become impossible to ignore. Several museums have now agreed to send back items whose acquisition was clearly unlawful by any standard, and a few governments have changed their laws to make this easier. Opponents of large-scale restitution advance a range of arguments. Some claim that the objects are better protected in wealthy institutions with sophisticated conservation facilities, an argument that critics regard as patronising, given that many countries requesting their return have well-equipped museums of their own. Others argue that 'universal' museums allow audiences to compare cultures side by side, an educational benefit that would be lost if collections were dispersed. A more pragmatic concern is precedent: if one object is returned, where does the process end? The debate is unlikely to be resolved by a single principle. Each case involves different histories, different legal frameworks and different claims of ownership. What has changed, perhaps irreversibly, is the burden of proof. Whereas museums once assumed that possession implied legitimacy, they are now increasingly expected to demonstrate how each object came into their care, and to engage seriously with those who believe it was taken from them.

passage.title: The Invention of Standard Time
passage.text: It is difficult today to imagine a world in which every town kept its own time, yet until the second half of the nineteenth century that was precisely the situation in most countries. Clocks were set according to the position of the sun, so that noon in a western city might arrive several minutes later than noon in a city further east. For most people, whose lives rarely took them beyond walking distance of home, the discrepancy hardly mattered. It was the railway that changed everything. As trains began to connect distant cities, timetables became a nightmare of conversions. A traveller crossing a country might pass through dozens of local times, and the risk of collisions on single-track lines made the confusion more than a mere inconvenience. Railway companies responded by adopting a single standard time across their networks, and in many places the public gradually followed, often with considerable reluctance. Some critics complained that it was absurd for a city to set its clocks by the time in a distant capital; others regarded the change as an arrogant imposition by commercial interests on the natural order. In 1884, an international conference agreed on a system of time zones based on a prime meridian, though it took decades for many countries to adopt it fully. The episode offers a revealing example of how technology can reshape something as apparently fundamental as our experience of time. Standard time was not discovered; it was invented, negotiated and, at times, resisted. It is worth bearing this in mind whenever a new technology is described as simply inevitable. The digital networks that now synchronise our devices to the millisecond have, in their turn, altered our expectations of punctuality and availability in ways that earlier generations would have found equally strange.

passage.title: The Four-Day Week
passage.text: When a number of companies in Britain agreed to trial a four-day working week without any reduction in pay, sceptics predicted chaos. Productivity, they argued, would inevitably fall, customers would be neglected and the experiment would quietly be abandoned. Six months later, the results told a different story. The vast majority of participating firms chose to continue with the new arrangement, reporting that output had remained stable or even improved, while staff sickness and resignations had fallen noticeably. Employees described feeling less exhausted, more focused at work and better able to manage responsibilities at home. How can people produce as much in four days as in five? Part of the answer lies in how time was previously being used. Many organisations discovered that a considerable proportion of the working week had been consumed by unnecessary meetings, unproductive email exchanges and what one manager described as 'performative busyness'. Faced with a shorter week, teams were forced to prioritise ruthlessly, cutting tasks that added little value. Nevertheless, enthusiasts should be wary of overstating the case. The companies involved volunteered to take part and were therefore likely to be well suited to the experiment; most were in office-based sectors where output is relatively easy to reorganise. Whether the same benefits could be achieved in hospitals, schools or factories, where work is tied to fixed shifts and physical presence, remains far from certain. There is also a risk that compressing work into fewer days simply intensifies it, replacing one form of exhaustion with another. Still, the trial has shifted the terms of the debate. The question is no longer whether a shorter week is conceivable, but under what conditions it can succeed. For a working culture that has long equated long hours with commitment, that alone represents a significant change.

passage.title: Switching Off the News
passage.text: A paradox has emerged in surveys of news consumption. Never before has so much information been so easily available, yet a growing proportion of people report that they deliberately avoid the news, either occasionally or altogether. The phenomenon, sometimes called 'news avoidance', is not confined to those with little interest in current affairs. Many of the people who switch off describe themselves as having once been avid followers of events, and their reasons are strikingly consistent. The news, they say, is overwhelmingly negative, leaves them feeling powerless and has a damaging effect on their mood. Some also express distrust, believing that coverage is biased or sensationalised. From the perspective of individual wellbeing, it is hard to argue with their choice. Research has linked heavy consumption of distressing news to increased anxiety, and there is little evidence that constant exposure makes people better informed in any meaningful sense. A headline glimpsed on a phone while queuing for coffee rarely deepens understanding. From the perspective of democracy, however, the trend is more troubling. Societies depend on citizens who are sufficiently informed to vote, debate and hold those in power to account. If the most disillusioned simply withdraw, public discussion may become dominated by the most partisan voices. Some news organisations have begun to respond. So-called 'constructive journalism' aims to report problems alongside possible solutions, without sliding into naive optimism. Others are experimenting with slower formats, such as weekly summaries and in-depth explanatory pieces, that prioritise context over immediacy. Whether such approaches can win back those who have switched off remains to be seen. What seems clear is that the problem is not simply one of supply. People have not lost interest in the world; many have lost faith that following the news, in its current form, helps them understand it.

passage.title: The Power of Belief
passage.text: The placebo effect has long been treated by medical researchers as something of a nuisance. In clinical trials, new drugs must outperform a dummy pill precisely because patients who believe they are receiving treatment often report genuine improvement, even when the pill contains nothing but sugar. For decades, this was regarded as a sign that symptoms had been partly imaginary, or that patients were simply telling doctors what they wanted to hear. More recent research has painted a considerably more intriguing picture. Brain scans have shown that placebos can trigger the release of the body's own pain-relieving chemicals, producing measurable physiological changes rather than mere shifts in perception. The context in which treatment is given also appears to matter enormously. Larger pills tend to be more effective than smaller ones, injections more effective than tablets and expensive placebos more effective than cheap ones. Even the warmth and attentiveness of the doctor can influence outcomes. Most surprising of all are studies of so-called 'open-label' placebos, in which patients are told explicitly that the pills they are taking contain no active ingredient. Remarkably, some patients with conditions such as chronic back pain or irritable bowel syndrome still report significant relief. Researchers suspect that the ritual of taking a pill, combined with the expectation of care, may be sufficient to activate the body's own healing mechanisms. None of this suggests that placebos can cure serious diseases or replace effective medicine; their effects are generally limited to symptoms such as pain, nausea and fatigue. Nevertheless, the findings raise uncomfortable questions for healthcare systems that increasingly reduce consultations to a few hurried minutes. If the manner in which treatment is delivered can itself contribute to recovery, then time and compassion may be less a luxury than a legitimate part of medicine.

passage.title: Meat Without Animals
passage.text: Cultivated meat, grown from animal cells in large steel vessels rather than raised on farms, has been described as one of the most promising technologies of the century. Its supporters argue that it could provide the protein that a growing global population demands while drastically reducing the environmental damage caused by livestock farming, which is responsible for a substantial share of greenhouse gas emissions and deforestation. It would also, they point out, remove the need to slaughter billions of animals each year. The first cultivated burger, unveiled over a decade ago, cost hundreds of thousands of dollars to produce. Since then, costs have fallen dramatically, and in a handful of countries cultivated chicken has been approved for sale. Yet the technology still faces formidable obstacles before it can compete with conventional meat on a large scale. Growing cells requires a nutrient-rich medium that remains expensive, and producing it in vast quantities without contamination is a major engineering challenge. Some analysts have also questioned the environmental claims, noting that the energy required to run large bioreactors could, if supplied by fossil fuels, cancel out much of the climate benefit. Then there is the question of whether consumers will actually want it. Surveys suggest that attitudes vary widely. Younger, urban consumers tend to express curiosity, while others are put off by the idea of meat produced in a laboratory, regarding it as unnatural. Some farming organisations have lobbied for restrictions on the use of words such as 'meat' on packaging, and at least one government has banned the product outright. Ultimately, the future of cultivated meat may depend less on scientific breakthroughs than on politics and perception. A product that is cheaper, tastier and greener than its rivals might still struggle if consumers cannot be persuaded to trust it.

passage.title: Meat Without Animals
passage.text: Cultivated meat, grown from animal cells in large steel vessels rather than raised on farms, has been described as one of the most promising technologies of the century. Its supporters argue that it could provide the protein that a growing global population demands while drastically reducing the environmental damage caused by livestock farming, which is responsible for a substantial share of greenhouse gas emissions and deforestation. It would also, they point out, remove the need to slaughter billions of animals each year. The first cultivated burger, unveiled over a decade ago, cost hundreds of thousands of dollars to produce. Since then, costs have fallen dramatically, and in a handful of countries cultivated chicken has been approved for sale. Growing cells requires a nutrient-rich medium that remains expensive, and producing it in vast quantities without contamination is a major engineering challenge. Younger, urban consumers tend to express curiosity, while others are put off by the idea of meat produced in a laboratory, regarding it as unnatural. passage.title: A Gentle Push
passage.text: Governments have traditionally relied on two main tools to change behaviour: laws that forbid or require certain actions, and financial incentives such as taxes and subsidies. Over the past two decades, a third approach has become increasingly influential. Known as 'nudging', it draws on insights from behavioural science to steer people towards better choices without restricting their freedom or significantly altering their economic incentives. The classic examples are deceptively simple. When employees are automatically enrolled in a pension scheme, with the option to leave if they wish, participation rises dramatically compared with schemes that require people to sign up actively. Placing healthy food at eye level in school canteens increases the number of children who choose it. Letters informing taxpayers that most of their neighbours pay on time have been shown to improve payment rates. In each case, the decision remains entirely with the individual; what changes is the way the choice is presented. The appeal to policymakers is obvious. Nudges tend to be cheap, politically uncontroversial and easy to test. Yet the approach has attracted criticism from several directions. Some argue that it is subtly manipulative, exploiting psychological weaknesses rather than engaging people's capacity to reason. If a government knows that most people will not change a default setting, is it really respecting their choice? Others make the opposite complaint: that nudges are too weak to tackle large problems such as climate change or obesity, and that their popularity may distract from the tougher regulation that is genuinely needed. There is some evidence for this second concern; recent analyses suggest that the effects of many nudges are smaller than early studies implied. The fairest conclusion may be that nudging is a useful addition to the policymaker's toolkit, but not a substitute for it. A gentle push can help, but some problems require more than a push.

passage.title: The Vanishing Night
passage.text: For most of human history, a clear night sky offered a spectacle of thousands of stars and the pale band of the Milky Way. Today, an estimated eight out of ten people in Europe and North America live where that view has been erased by artificial light. Light pollution, as it is known, has long been dismissed as an aesthetic concern, a regrettable but minor side effect of modern life. Mounting evidence suggests that it is considerably more serious. Many species have evolved to rely on natural cycles of light and darkness. Newly hatched sea turtles, which instinctively head towards the brightest horizon, are lured inland by coastal lighting instead of towards the sea. Migrating birds become disoriented by illuminated buildings, with fatal consequences on a vast scale. Insects, drawn to streetlights in enormous numbers, are thought to be contributing to the alarming decline in their populations, with knock-on effects throughout food chains. Humans are not immune. Exposure to artificial light at night can suppress the production of melatonin, the hormone that regulates sleep, and some studies have tentatively linked night-time light exposure to a range of health problems, though establishing direct causes remains difficult. Unlike many environmental problems, however, light pollution is remarkably easy to reverse. It requires no technological breakthrough and leaves no lasting residue; switch off a light and the darkness returns immediately. Simple measures, such as shielding lamps so that light points downwards, using warmer colours and dimming lights late at night, can dramatically reduce the problem while saving energy. Several towns have obtained 'dark sky' status by adopting such measures, and some now attract tourists eager to see a night sky their grandparents took for granted. The obstacle, it seems, is less practical than psychological: a deep-rooted association between brightness, safety and progress that has rarely been questioned.

passage.title: The Greenest Building
passage.text: When we think of environmentally friendly architecture, we tend to picture gleaming new structures covered in solar panels, with triple-glazed windows and rooftop gardens. Yet many architects now argue that the greenest building is often the one that already exists. The reasoning lies in a concept known as 'embodied carbon': the emissions produced in extracting, manufacturing and transporting building materials, and in the construction process itself. Concrete and steel, the backbone of most modern buildings, are particularly carbon-intensive. Studies suggest that even a highly energy-efficient new building may take several decades to compensate, through lower running costs, for the carbon released during its construction. Demolishing a sound building and replacing it, in other words, can do more environmental harm than good. This has fuelled growing interest in adaptive reuse, the practice of converting old buildings for new purposes. Disused factories have become apartments, power stations have been transformed into art galleries and churches into libraries. Beyond the environmental benefits, such projects often preserve a sense of local history and identity that new developments struggle to replicate. Adaptive reuse is not without its difficulties. Older buildings may contain hazardous materials, fail to meet modern safety standards or have layouts poorly suited to contemporary needs. Renovation can also be unpredictable; hidden structural problems frequently emerge only once work has begun, pushing up costs. Developers, moreover, often find it simpler and more profitable to start from scratch, particularly since tax systems in many countries treat new construction more favourably than renovation. Changing this may require policy as much as architectural ingenuity. Some cities have begun to require developers to assess the carbon cost of demolition before permission is granted. Such measures signal a shift in thinking: the question is no longer only how efficiently a building will perform, but whether it needs to be built at all.

passage.title: Beyond Ten Thousand Hours
passage.text: Few ideas about expertise have spread as widely as the claim that ten thousand hours of practice will make anyone a master of their field. The figure, popularised by bestselling books, was derived from research on violinists, which found that the most accomplished students had, by their early twenties, accumulated far more hours of practice than their less successful peers. The message was appealingly democratic: talent, it implied, matters far less than effort. The researcher behind the original study, however, later expressed frustration at how his work had been interpreted. The number itself, he pointed out, was an average rather than a threshold, and varied considerably between individuals and disciplines. More importantly, the research emphasised not just the quantity of practice but its quality. What he called 'deliberate practice' involves working at the edge of one's ability, with clear goals, immediate feedback and, typically, the guidance of a skilled teacher. Simply repeating a familiar activity for thousands of hours, as anyone who has played the same few songs on the guitar for years will know, produces little improvement. Subsequent research has complicated the picture further. Several large analyses have found that practice, while important, accounts for only part of the differences in performance between individuals, and that its contribution varies enormously by field. In highly structured activities such as chess or classical music, practice explains a good deal; in less predictable domains, such as many professions, far less. passage.title: The Right to Be Forgotten
passage.text: In the age before the internet, embarrassing episodes from a person's past tended to fade naturally. A minor conviction, an unwise remark or a business failure might be recorded in an old newspaper, but finding it required considerable effort. Today, a few keystrokes can retrieve information from decades ago and present it to a potential employer, landlord or partner as if it were current. It was in response to this situation that European courts established what has become known as the 'right to be forgotten'. Under this principle, individuals can ask search engines to remove links to information about them that is inaccurate, irrelevant or no longer relevant, provided there is no overriding public interest in keeping it accessible. The information itself is not deleted from the original source; it simply becomes harder to find through a search of the person's name. Supporters regard the right as an essential protection of privacy and dignity. People change, they argue, and should not be permanently defined by their worst moments. A teenager's foolish post or a debt long since repaid should not follow someone for the rest of their life. Critics, however, see a threat to freedom of expression and the public's right to know. Journalists have expressed concern that the right could be used by powerful people to bury unflattering but legitimate stories, and some have objected to private companies being placed in the position of judging what the public interest requires. There are also practical complications: the internet does not respect national borders, and information removed in one country may remain accessible elsewhere. The underlying dilemma is unlikely to disappear. Both privacy and transparency are genuine values, and in a world where nothing is ever truly forgotten, deciding which should prevail in each case will remain a matter of difficult judgement rather than simple rules.

passage.title: In Praise of Boredom
passage.text: Boredom has an unenviable reputation. We associate it with wasted time, restlessness and a vague sense of dissatisfaction, and most of us go to considerable lengths to avoid it. With a smartphone in almost every pocket, the empty moments that once punctuated daily life, waiting for a bus, standing in a queue, sitting in a doctor's waiting room, can now be filled instantly. It is worth asking, however, whether something valuable is being lost in the process. A number of psychologists have argued that boredom serves a useful function. Far from being merely unpleasant, it acts as a signal that our current activity is not meeting our needs, prompting us to seek something more meaningful or stimulating. In this sense, it resembles pain or hunger: uncomfortable, but informative. Some intriguing experiments have also suggested a link between boredom and creativity. In one study, participants who first completed a deliberately tedious task, such as copying numbers from a telephone directory, subsequently came up with more inventive ideas in a creative-thinking test than those who had not. The researchers speculated that boredom encourages the mind to wander, and that daydreaming allows unexpected connections to form. It would be unwise to overstate these findings. The studies were relatively small, and chronic boredom, particularly among those with few opportunities for meaningful activity, is associated with genuinely harmful outcomes, from depression to risky behaviour. Boredom is not, in itself, a virtue. Nevertheless, the habit of reaching for a screen at the first hint of tedium may deprive us of the mental space in which reflection and imagination flourish. The challenge, perhaps, is not to seek out boredom deliberately, but to resist the reflex that eliminates it before it has had a chance to do its work.
